n: Deborah and Barak celebrate the victory in song. This poem is considered one of the oldest passages in the Bible, and its archaic Hebrew is hard to translate in places.
The song opens with praise: leaders took the lead and the people volunteered freely. Willing hearts are a theme of the whole poem.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; possibly “when leaders took the lead” or “when locks were loosed” (warriors’ flowing hair).

n: Deborah calls foreign kings to listen as she sings to Israel’s God. Their power means nothing beside His.
She pictures the Lord marching from Seir and Edom in the south — the region of Sinai — with the earth shaking and clouds pouring rain. The storm at the Kishon was God’s coming.

f.w: when thou wentest out of Seir

n: Mountains quake before Him, as Sinai did when the law was given. The God of Sinai is the God fighting for Israel now.

f.g: Possibly “the One of Sinai,” a title for God.

n: Before the victory, roads were too dangerous to use; travelers took back paths. Life under oppression was fearful and hidden.

f.g: Side roads, winding paths.

n: Village life collapsed until Deborah arose as “a mother in Israel” — a protector and nurturer of the nation.

f.g: Possibly “the peasantry” or “leadership” ceased; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: Choosing new gods brought war to their gates. Israel was so disarmed that hardly a shield or spear could be found.

f.g: At the city gates — war at their very doors.

n: Deborah honors the leaders who volunteered and calls for praise to the Lord.

f.g: Commanders, leaders.
Praise the Lord.

n: Everyone — the wealthy who ride white donkeys, those in authority, and ordinary travelers — should tell what happened.

f.g: Light-colored donkeys, ridden by people of rank.

n: At the wells, once dangerous, people now retell the Lord’s righteous acts. Israel can return to its city gates in peace.

f.g: Wells, where people gathered and where raiders once struck.
Recount, repeat.
Hebrew tsidqot YHWH, His saving acts or victories.

n: A call to action: wake up, Deborah, and sing! Rise, Barak, and lead away your captives. Scripture later uses “lead captivity captive” for Christ’s victory.
The surviving faithful remnant came down to rule over the powerful. The Lord gave the weak victory over the mighty.

f.g: The survivors, the remnant.

n: The song now praises the tribes that came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (Manasseh), and Zebulun — even its record-keepers.

f.w: they that handle the pen of the writer
f.g: Possibly officers who held a commander’s staff or scribes who mustered troops.

n: Issachar’s leaders joined Deborah and rushed into the valley behind Barak. But Reuben debated endlessly instead of acting.

f.g: Long deliberation — much thinking, no action.

n: A pointed question to Reuben: why stay among your flocks listening to the sheep? They had good intentions but stayed home.

f.g: Sheep pens; possibly campfires or saddlebags.

n: Gilead, Dan, and Asher also stayed away — busy with land, ships, and harbors. The song names those who didn’t show up.

f.g: Dan may have worked in the coastal shipping trade.
Inlets or harbors.

n: Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives on the battlefield — they get the highest praise.

f.g: Risked.
The heights of the battleground.

n: The Canaanite kings fought at Taanach by Megiddo’s waters but won no plunder.

f.w: Taanach by the waters of Megiddo
they took no gain of money
f.g: They carried off no silver as spoil.

n: Heaven itself fought against Sisera. The stars, often linked to rain in ancient thought, joined the battle — a poetic way of saying God sent the storm.

f.g: The stars on their paths across the sky.

n: The flooded Kishon swept away the enemy. Deborah urges her own soul to march on in strength.

f.w: O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength
f.g: Or “March on, my soul, with might.”

n: The poem’s rhythm imitates galloping horses fleeing in panic.

f.g: Gallopings, dashings.

n: A curse on Meroz, a town that refused to help. Failing to stand with the Lord’s cause in a crisis was itself a serious failure.

f.g: An unknown town, probably near the battlefield.

f.w: to the help of the LORD
f.g: To support the Lord’s cause and people.

n: In contrast, Jael is “blessed above women.” Similar words are later spoken of Mary.
Sisera asked for water; she gave him rich milk in a fine bowl. Hospitality turned into a trap.

f.g: Curdled milk or yogurt, not butter in the modern sense.
A bowl fit for nobles.

n: Jael grabs the tent peg and workman’s mallet and strikes Sisera through the temple.

f.g: Better “crushed his head”; compare chapter 4.

n: The repeated words slow time down as the mighty general sinks and falls dead at a woman’s feet. Some see an echo of the promise that the serpent’s head would be crushed.
The scene shifts to Sisera’s mother at her window, anxiously wondering why her son’s chariot is so late.

f.g: A latticed window.
Delay.

n: Her wise ladies answer, and she repeats their comfort to herself.

f.g: Noblewomen attending her.

n: They imagine Sisera dividing loot: captive women and embroidered cloth. The irony is painful — the women of Israel were spared because he lies dead.

f.g: Succeeded.
Literally “a womb or two,” a crude soldier’s phrase for captive women.
Dyed, many-colored garments.

n: The song ends with a prayer: may God’s enemies perish, but may those who love Him shine like the rising sun. Forty years of peace follow.

f.w: as the sun when he goeth forth in his might
